title: Aurangzeb Era Revenue and Military Pressure in Bengal
subtitle: Campaigns on Bengal’s northeastern and southeastern frontiers coincided with growing demands on the province’s revenues.
summary: Aurangzeb appointed Mir Jumla governor of Bengal in 1660. Jadunath Sarkar’s account describes his campaigns in Cooch Behar and Assam from late 1661 and his effort to reorganize Bengal’s fleet and administration. Shaista Khan’s forces captured Chittagong in 1666 after operations against Arakanese and Portuguese-Magh maritime power. Sarkar also reports that Shaista Khan began sending five lakh rupees annually to the emperor in 1682. Banglapedia records Murshid Quli Khan’s appointment as Bengal’s diwan in 1701 and a regular annual remittance of one crore rupees beginning in 1702. These sources outline imperial extraction and military pressures but do not establish how the fiscal demands were distributed among Bengal’s inhabitants.
heroTagline: Frontier campaigns and an imperial revenue stream, 1660–1702
whyItMatters: The campaign record shows Bengal’s governors directing armies and fleets toward Cooch Behar, Assam, and Chittagong, while the reported remittances connect provincial finance to Aurangzeb’s imperial court. The evidence available here gives only a broad outline of those transfers; it does not document their incidence or quantify the burdens on cultivators and other residents.
